cognate: Ved. āmá- ~ Gk ὠμός 'raw' (*h₂eh₃mó-) qualifying Ved. kravís- ~ Gk κρέας 'raw flesh, meat' (*kréwh₂-s); verb of eating Ved. ad- ~ Gk ἔδω (*h₁ed-); and the compound 'raw-eater' Ved. āmā́d- ~ Gk ὠμηστής (*h₂eh₃mo- + *h₁ed-).
drift_or_renewal: Head noun partly renewed in AVŚ 8.6.48 (āmaṃ māṃsam, with kraviḥ in the parallel colon); RV 1.162.10 keeps the full pair āmásya kravíṣaḥ. Vedic kravís- narrowed to 'raw/bloody flesh, gore', Greek κρέας generalised to 'meat'. Verb of cooking renewed (Ved. pac-, Gk ἕψω/ὀπτάω).
shared_syntax: attributive adjective 'raw' + noun 'flesh' (āmásya kravíṣaḥ / ὠμὰ κρέα, ὠμῶν κρεῶν), as object of 'eat' (āmaṃ māṃsam adanti / ὤμ̓ κρέα ἔδμεναι); the same pair also compounds into an agent noun 'raw-eater' (āmā́d- / ὠμηστής).
context: In both traditions raw flesh is what is set against cooked, sacrificial or civilised food. RV 1.162.10 says the smell of raw flesh must be made well-cooked by the slaughterers; Od. 12.396 has roasted and raw meat; the Hippocratic passage gives boiled meat instead of raw as the step from the primitive diet. Eating raw flesh marks demons and beasts: AV kravyād/āmād demons and raw-eating vultures on corpses (AVŚ 11.10.18) ~ Homeric ὠμησταί birds and dogs tearing the slain (Il. 11.454, 22.67), Achilles' wish to eat Hector raw (Il. 22.347), Achilles called ὠμηστής (Il. 24.207). The two cognate words and their compound recur in the same pairing and with the same value; it is not merely that both languages have a word for raw.

cognate: Lat. mel ~ Gk μέλι (*mélit) with Lat. dulcis ~ Gk γλυκύς (*dl(e)ukú-), in the comparative of 'sweet'.
shared_syntax: comparative of 'sweet' with honey as the standard: melle dulci dulcior ~ μέλιτος γλυκίων (Hom.), and Xenophanes' figs γλύσσονα measured against honey; attributive 'sweet honey' dulce mel ~ μέλι γλυκερόν.
context: Sweetness measured against honey, said of a beloved (Plautus), of speech (Il. 1.249 Nestor, Il. 18.109 anger) and of fruit (Xenophanes). Weak: the comparison is close to universal and these are the ordinary words for honey and sweet in both languages, so the lexicon alone predicts the match. Kept only as a Graeco-Latin cognate comparative figure.

note: Slab almost entirely Hippocratic medical prose pivots with Cato/Plautus/Lucretius/AV partners matched on common roots (wine, honey, seasons, ordinals); no inherited phraseology in most bundles. Considered and rejected: θέρος/χειμών ~ ghraṃsa/hima merism (generic), οἶνος μέλας ~ uinum atrum (renewal, generic), lick+honey leyǵʰ- (Gk/Lat/Ved, generic), frigus ad ossa ~ ῥιγεῖ ὀστώδεα (generic), ordinal series (not phraseology).
